content: The severity of symptoms associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has been hypothesized to have a positive correlation with the levels of circulating or stored toxic metals in the body. It has also been proposed that the removal of these heavy metals through the use of pharmaceutical chelating agents could lead to an improvement in ASD symptoms. The objective of this review was to evaluate both the potential benefits and the adverse effects of pharmaceutical chelating agents, referred to as chelation therapy, in the treatment of ASD symptoms. A comprehensive search was conducted on November 6, 2014, across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and CINAHL, as well as 15 additional databases and three clinical trial registries. References from relevant studies were also reviewed, and experts in the field were contacted for additional information. The inclusion criteria for this review were limited to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared pharmaceutical chelating agents with placebo in individuals diagnosed with ASD. Two independent reviewers selected studies, assessed their risk of bias, and extracted relevant data. However, a meta-analysis was not performed because only one study met the inclusion criteria. Nine studies were excluded from the review because they were either non-randomized trials or were withdrawn before participant enrollment. The single included study was conducted in two phases. In the first phase, 77 children with ASD were randomly assigned to receive either a glutathione lotion or a placebo lotion for seven days, followed by three days of oral dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA). Of these, 49 children who were identified as high excreters of heavy metals during the first phase proceeded to the second phase. In this phase, participants received three days of oral DMSA or placebo, followed by an 11-day break, with this cycle repeated up to six times. The second phase aimed to evaluate the efficacy of multiple doses of oral DMSA compared to placebo in children who were high excreters of heavy metals. The results of the study showed no evidence to support the claim that multiple rounds of oral DMSA had any effect on improving ASD symptoms. The authors concluded that this review was based on data from only one study, which had significant methodological limitations. As a result, there is no clinical trial evidence to suggest that pharmaceutical chelation is an effective treatment for ASD. Furthermore, previous reports of serious adverse events associated with chelation therapy, including hypocalcemia, renal impairment, and even death, indicate that the risks of using chelation therapy for ASD currently outweigh any proven benefits. Before further clinical trials are conducted, it is essential to establish evidence supporting a causal relationship between heavy metals and autism, as well as to develop methods that ensure the safety of participants.
